nameStory: The name 'Marsh Tickseed' tells you exactly where to find this plant and what to expect from it! It loves wet, marshy places, and like other tickseeds, it produces small seeds that can stick to your clothes. The 'beggarticks' nickname comes from how these clingy seeds seem to beg for a ride on passing animals and humans.
description: Marsh Tickseed is a tall, cheerful annual wildflower that can tower up to 5 feet high in wet places. It produces bright yellow daisy-like flowers with both a central disc and radiating petals, looking like sunny little faces bobbing above the marsh grass. This native plant is perfectly adapted to life in soggy soils where many other flowers would struggle. Despite its impressive height, it completes its entire life cycle in just one growing season.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow daisy-like blooms with both a central button of tiny disc flowers and cheerful radiating petals that feel papery to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Impressively tall annual that can reach 5 feet, with a sturdy upright stem that feels substantial but hollow when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, narrow seeds with barbed tips that grab onto clothing and fur with surprising tenacity - you'll feel them catch as you brush past

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found with 'wet feet' in marshes, swamps, and shoreline areas where the soil squishes underfoot

habitat: Look for Marsh Tickseed in New England's wettest spots - freshwater marshes, swampy areas, and along pond and stream edges where the ground stays soggy. It thrives in the rich, mucky soils of estuaries and wetland margins, often growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll rarely find it far from water, as it needs consistently wet conditions to flourish.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge from muddy soil as temperatures warm, starting as small green shoots that quickly gain height through late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time brings masses of bright yellow flowers that attract bees and butterflies throughout the warmest months.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and produce the characteristic 'beggartick' seeds that readily attach to clothing and animal fur for dispersal before frost kills the plant.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the entire plant dies back, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring - no above-ground parts remain.

funFact: Marsh Tickseed is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only twice in recent botanical surveys, making it one of the region's most elusive native wildflowers - finding one would be like discovering botanical treasure!
confusionNotes: With 14 different beggarticks species in New England, telling them apart can be tricky! The key is habitat - if you're seeing tall yellow daisy-like flowers specifically in marshes and wet areas, you're likely looking at Marsh Tickseed rather than its drier-soil cousins like Devil's Beggarticks.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'beggarticks' fool you into thinking this is some kind of pest - it's actually a valuable native wildflower that provides food for pollinators and birds. The 'ticks' refer only to the seed's hitchhiking ability, not to any blood-sucking insects!
compareHints: Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions. It's also among the tallest in the family, often outgrowing other beggarticks species. The combination of impressive height and marsh habitat makes it fairly distinctive once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
